Cyber-JEV: Matched Contrastive Fine-Tuning of Language Models for Fast Source-Code Vulnerability TriageThanks: *Zhuyi Zhao and Shengjie Yuan contributed equally to this work and are co-first authors.

Zhuyi Zhao*, Shengjie Yuan*, Shengyu Wang, Kang Wei,
Wang Yang, Wenchao Xu, Fushuo Huo Affiliation: 
Abstract

Single-pass scoring models such as Jev give each code function a vulnerability probability, so that security teams can rank many functions for review without generating written explanations. Training an open-weight model for this task is limited by data. Benchmarks with both vulnerable and non-vulnerable labels keep few vulnerable functions once examples related to the test data are removed, while larger public vulnerability records mostly contain vulnerable functions only. Mixing the two lets the data source predict the label, and training on the labeled data alone leaves a model that often scores a fixed function above its vulnerable original. We present Cyber-JEV, a fine-tuning method that uses fix commits to turn these records into comparison groups. Each group holds a vulnerable function, its patched version and up to two unchanged functions from the same file, so the model sees the change that removed a recorded defect. One shared model learns two tasks: classifying functions from the labeled reference data, and ranking the vulnerable function above the other members of its group. At test time the input is one function and the output is a vulnerability score. On a test benchmark of 7,270 functions, an ensemble of five fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B models reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.814, compared with 0.743 for Jev 1.13. With the 4,031 alerts of Jev as the review budget, it misses 16 of 322 vulnerable functions instead of 39. Compared with training on the reference data alone, it ranks the vulnerable version above the patched version 14.8 to 29.2 percentage points more often on three sets of real fixes. Such scores can order the changed functions of a pull request or a release for review under a fixed budget.

Index Terms: 
source-code vulnerability triage, probabilistic decision models, contrastive fine-tuning, shortcut learning, patch sensitivity, language models

I Introduction

Modern continuous integration and pre-release security auditing workflows must screen thousands of modified functions under tight latency and analyst review budgets. Rather than relying on slow multi-turn chain-of-thought generation, fast probabilistic decision language models—exemplified by TypeSafe AI’s Jev [1, 2]—provide a streamlined single-pass interface: given a candidate function, the model outputs a calibrated vulnerability probability in a single forward pass, allowing automated pipelines to prioritize high-risk functions or trigger human review.

Extending this fast decision paradigm to source-code vulnerability triage, however, faces two competing training bottlenecks [3, 4, 5]. The first bottleneck is source shortcut learning when aggregating public security data. After standard cross-project and near-duplicate deduplication hygiene is enforced between training and evaluation splits [6, 7, 8, 9], clean benchmark pools retain very few vulnerable positives (only 197 functions in our setup). Augmenting training with public security patch archives such as MoreFixes [10] and MegaVul [11] contributes thousands of real vulnerabilities, yet the records we admit from these archives contain only vulnerable functions and no benign negatives. Naive joint training allows repository provenance to give away the label: a classifier can minimize training loss simply by recognizing project formatting and identifier conventions, causing test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) to drop to 0.602—worse than ranking functions purely by byte length.

The second bottleneck is an inherent anti-patch bias. If external patch archives are simply discarded in favor of standard binary cross-entropy fine-tuning on the clean reference pool, the model attains strong macroscopic ranking (0.804 AUROC) but systematically fails on minimal security fixes: in 67.2% of vulnerability-versus-patch pairs, it assigns a higher vulnerability score to the patched code than to the original vulnerable code (mirroring the 60.5% inversion rate of the unadapted base model). A likely reason is that security patches typically insert bounds checks, null-pointer guards, or error-return branches, so standard cross-entropy may teach the model to flag high-risk code modules broadly while mistaking newly added defensive checks for risk indicators.

Existing distributionally robust optimization [12], invariant risk minimization [13], and prior-shift logit adjustment [14] all require both positive and negative examples within every source, and thus can neither construct missing within-source negatives nor teach fine-grained patch discrimination. Our approach draws inspiration from classical matched statistical designs and modern contrastive learning: matched sampling in statistics (such as classical case-control studies [15]) eliminates shared group bias via conditional likelihood [16, 17] while relying on a representative reference sample to anchor baseline probabilities [18, 19]; meanwhile, counterfactual minimal edits [20] and hard-negative contrastive ranking [21, 22, 23] directly train neural encoders to detect subtle semantic changes.

Guided by these insights, we introduce Cyber-JEV, adapting the open-weight Qwen3.5-4B model [24] for fast, calibrated, and patch-sensitive source-code vulnerability triage (Fig. 1). At the data level, we develop Provenance-Matched Completion (PMC), a five-stage curation and sanitization pipeline that extracts dual-hash and abstract syntax tree (AST) verified patched versions and unchanged same-file context functions from security commits. At the training level, we propose Anchored-Contrastive Hybrid Loss (HYB), which orthogonally decouples global scale calibration from within-group defect ranking, supported by a two-pass memory-bounded gradient accumulator for long functions.

Our contribution is Cyber-JEV, a fine-tuning method in which PMC converts 17 positive-only patch archives into hash-verified groups of vulnerable, patched, and unchanged same-file functions and HYB trains these groups only through within-group ranking while keeping cross-entropy on the reference pool, yielding a five-model ensemble that outperforms Jev 1.13 on all four ranking metrics across 7,270 functions and ranks vulnerable code above its patched version more often than reference-pool fine-tuning on three patch suites, including two from TitanVul.

II Structured Contrastive Dataset Curation and Sanitization

Public Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records and patch repositories offer diverse examples of real-world defects, yet most extract only vulnerable functions alongside truncated spans and near-duplicate clones. PMC transforms heterogeneous raw archives into clean contrastive supervision through five sequential stages.

II-A Stage 1: Multi-Source Collection and Cross-Split Hygiene

Starting from 148,462 candidate functions, Stage 1 aggregates two complementary source categories: (i) a natural reference pool ℛ\mathcal{R} drawn from three benchmarks containing both natural positives and negatives—PrimeVul [8], DiverseVul [25], and CVEfixes [26]; and (ii) 17 external security patch archives 𝒯\mathcal{T}—including MoreFixes [10], MegaVul [11], ARVO [27], CrossVul [28], ReposVul [29], and curated National Vulnerability Database (NVD) commit collections.

To uphold strict evaluation hygiene, we build an undirected association graph across all training candidates and protected validation, calibration, and test splits: two functions are linked if they share a normalized open-source project family, CVE identifier, Git fix commit hash, exact code hash (under raw, whitespace-normalized, or comment-stripped lexical forms), or 128-bit token-shingle Jaccard similarity of at least 0.8, and only connected components completely disjoint from evaluation splits are admitted to training. After deduplication, reference pool ℛ\mathcal{R} contains 197 vulnerable positives and 5,026 benign negatives, while the 17 external archives 𝒯\mathcal{T} contribute 3,357 vulnerable positives and zero negatives (top two rows of Table II). Naively merging ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} causes the normalized mutual information (NMI) between source identity and label, I⁡(S,Y)/H⁡(Y)I(S;Y)/H(Y), to reach 87.3%.

II-B Stages 2 to 5: Provenance-Matched Completion and Cleaning

To eliminate source predictability and supply fine-grained repair contrasts, PMC executes four reconstruction and sanitization stages:

Stage 2: Cryptographic Git Verification and Zero-Truncation Parsing. Raw commit datasets frequently suffer from missing file snapshots or broken spans. For each security commit, PMC verifies both the Git object blob SHA-1 and file content SHA-256 of pre-fix and post-fix files, then applies pinned tree-sitter grammars to extract complete, syntax-error-free function definitions (150 to 24,000 bytes) that fit entirely within the prompt window without token truncation. For the 725 positives that do not yield a verified non-empty group (including 660 MoreFixes entries that lack post-fix code), we enforce strict completeness gating: only the 2,829 positives that form verified non-empty contrast groups enter the contrastive ranking branch of HYB, whereas all 3,554 positives remain retained in full-data cross-entropy baselines so baselines receive maximum data volume. The 45 reference-pool positives without a group still enter the cross-entropy term of HYB, so HYB trains on 2,874 distinct positives (Table I).

Stage 3: Patched Version and Same-File Context Pairing. For each verified vulnerable function x+x^{+}, PMC constructs a provenance-matched contrast group G⁡(x+)G(x^{+}) (2,829 groups totaling 10,099 members, median size 4) comprising two complementary types of same-source negatives:

  1. 1.

    Patched version xpatchx^{\text{patch}} (present in 2,789 groups, combining 2,637 newly extracted counterparts and 152 reference-pool pairs; the remaining 40 groups pair x+x^{+} solely with verified same-file functions): the repaired version of the same function after the commit, isolating the minimal edit that resolves the vulnerability;

  2. 2.

    Unchanged same-file context functions {c1,…,cK}\{c_{1},\dots,c_{K}\} (deterministically sampled up to K=2K=2 per positive using a hash seed keyed to sample identity, or all available if fewer than two exist, totaling 4,481 functions): other functions in the same source file that remain byte-identical across the fix commit. Sharing headers, macros, and project style, they populate external archives with authentic benign context.

Stage 4: Near-Clone Conflict Sanitization for Weak Negatives. Because commit-derived negatives carry weak supervision, PMC screens every candidate patched and context function against all known vulnerable functions across the entire corpus via three-form SHA-256 matching and near-clone detection (Jaccard ≥0.8\geq 0.8), discarding any candidate matching a known defect (apart from a patched function’s own pre-fix counterpart). Furthermore, because external matched negatives enter HYB exclusively through within-group relative ranking rather than hard binary cross-entropy, rare unflagged minor flaws do not distort global calibration provided the actively patched defect carries higher acute risk.

Stage 5: Pre-Training Bias Audit and Held-Out Probe. As shown in Table II, pairing patched versions reduces source NMI from 87.3% to 31.5%, and adding K=2K=2 unchanged same-file functions lowers it to 14.0% with a near-neutral length-only AUROC of 0.574. We also hold out 1,924 never-trained unchanged same-file functions from external archives to audit cross-source false alarms.

III Decoupled Anchored-Contrastive Training Framework

Even with verified matched groups, standard loss functions struggle to jointly maintain global cross-project calibration and local patch sensitivity. We analyze this conflict and present our hybrid objective and memory-bounded gradient accumulator.

III-A Conflict Between Global Calibration and Local Sensitivity

Because repository formatting, macros, and naming styles expose provenance S⁡(X)S(X), Bayes’ rule decomposes the optimal training log-odds (logit) into two additive terms:

logit⁡Ptrain​(Y=1∣X)\displaystyle\operatorname{logit}P_{\text{train}}(Y{=}1\mid X) =logit⁡Ptrain​(Y=1∣S⁡(X))⏟α⁡(S⁡(X)):source style prior\displaystyle=\underbrace{\operatorname{logit}P_{\text{train}}(Y{=}1\mid S(X))}_{\alpha(S(X)):\ \text{source style prior}} (1)
+log⁡p⁡(X∣Y=1,S⁡(X))p⁡(X∣Y=0,S⁡(X))⏟β⁡(X):within-source defect contrast.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\log\frac{p(X\mid Y{=}1,S(X))}{p(X\mid Y{=}0,S(X))}}_{\beta(X):\ \text{within-source defect contrast}}.

Equation (1) explains why single-objective training fails at both ends. In uncompleted positive-only archives where Ptrain​(Y=0∣S⁡(X))=0P_{\text{train}}(Y{=}0\mid S(X))=0, the source prior α⁡(S⁡(X))\alpha(S(X)) diverges and overwhelms β⁡(X)\beta(X), injecting severe ranking noise on unseen test repositories. Even after PMC completion, applying standard cross-entropy across all rows forces the model to fit artificial group construction ratios (roughly 1:31{:}3 versus 4.4% natural prevalence), distorting global calibration; conversely, training solely with within-group ranking learns β⁡(X)\beta(X) but discards cross-repository baseline scale, leaving the model unable to compare a risky parser function in one project against a simple logging helper in another.

III-B Anchored-Contrastive Hybrid Loss

To resolve this dilemma, we combine the statistical principle of canceling group-specific repository style bias via conditional likelihood [16, 17] and anchoring baseline log-odds on a representative reference sample [18, 19] with InfoNCE contrastive ranking [21, 22].

Let sθ​(x)=ℓvuln​(x)−ℓbenign​(x)s_{\theta}(x)=\ell_{\text{vuln}}(x)-\ell_{\text{benign}}(x) denote the scalar decision margin output by the classification head for function xx. For a matched contrast group G={x0,x1,…,xm}G=\{x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\} with vulnerable function x0=x+x_{0}=x^{+} and matched negatives, we define the within-group contrastive ranking loss at temperature τ\tau (fixed to τ=1.0\tau=1.0 throughout):

ℒrank(G)=log∑j=0mexp(sθ(xj)/τ)−sθ(x0)/τ.\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(G)=\log\sum_{j=0}^{m}\exp\!\big(s_{\theta}(x_{j})/\tau\big)-s_{\theta}(x_{0})/\tau. (2)

Crucially, ℒrank​(G)\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(G) satisfies exact shift invariance to shared source biases: if sθ​(x)=aθ​(z)+gθ​(x)s_{\theta}(x)=a_{\theta}(z)+g_{\theta}(x), where aθ​(z)a_{\theta}(z) captures any bias from repository or file context zz, then because all members of GG come from the exact same commit and file, the shared factor exp⁡(aθ​(z)/τ)\exp(a_{\theta}(z)/\tau) cancels identically between numerator and denominator in (2). Memorizing a project-style offset shared by the group therefore yields no reduction in this loss, pushing the shared encoder toward within-group defect distinctions gθ​(x)g_{\theta}(x).

Denoting the reference-pool rows and matched groups sampled in an optimization step by ℛstep\mathcal{R}_{\text{step}} and 𝒢step\mathcal{G}_{\text{step}}, HYB orthogonally combines global anchoring with local ranking:

ℒHYB=∑i∈ℛstepwi​CEi∑i∈ℛstepwi+λ|𝒢step|​∑G∈𝒢stepℒrank​(G),\mathcal{L}_{\text{HYB}}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{\text{step}}}w_{i}\,\mathrm{CE}_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{\text{step}}}w_{i}}+\frac{\lambda}{|\mathcal{G}_{\text{step}}|}\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{step}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(G), (3)

where the first term computes class-balanced binary cross-entropy CEi\mathrm{CE}_{i} exclusively on natural reference pool ℛ\mathcal{R} with fixed weights (w1,w0)=(Nneg/Npos,1)(w_{1},w_{0})=(N_{\text{neg}}/N_{\text{pos}},1) so positive and negative classes carry equal total weight (shifting Bayes-optimal logits only by an order-preserving constant log⁡(w1/w0)\log(w_{1}/w_{0})), while the second term distributes all 2,829 verified contrast groups from ℛ∪𝒯\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{T} evenly across steps (default λ=1.0\lambda=1.0). Because external archives 𝒯\mathcal{T} never enter global cross-entropy, HYB acquires fine-grained patch sensitivity without importing source-prior skew.

III-C Memory-Bounded Two-Pass Group Gradient Accumulation

Complex vulnerable functions often span thousands of tokens. Evaluating (2) requires forward scores for all members of GG; for 4B-parameter models, roughly 7% of long-function groups exceed single-microbatch GPU memory.

To avoid truncating code or dropping long groups, we pair a group-preserving batcher with a two-pass gradient accumulator inspired by GradCache [30]. By the chain rule, the group loss gradient decomposes into a weighted sum of individual member gradients, ∇θℒrank​(G)=∑jcj​∇θsθ​(xj)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(G)=\sum_{j}c_{j}\nabla_{\theta}s_{\theta}(x_{j}) with cj=∂ℒrank​(G)/∂sθ​(xj)c_{j}=\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(G)/\partial s_{\theta}(x_{j}). Pass one evaluates oversized groups across microbatches without storing activation graphs to compute the scalar softmax coefficients cjc_{j}; pass two re-forwards each microbatch and backpropagates cj​sθ​(xj)c_{j}s_{\theta}(x_{j}), enabling zero-truncation group training within standard single-GPU memory limits. Because pass one runs in evaluation mode and pass two in training mode with LoRA dropout, this path approximates the exact group gradient.

IV Experimental Setup

IV-A Model Configuration and Multi-Seed Ensemble Interface

We fine-tune a frozen bf16 Qwen3.5-4B [24] backbone using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [31] (rank r=16r=16, α=32\alpha=32, training dropout 0.05) and a token-initialized binary classification head. All primary variants share an identical optimizer, cosine learning-rate schedule, and three-epoch budget (about 64 functions per step).

Hyperparameter locking and threshold calibration use an independent 512-function validation and calibration split with zero test-label exposure. To stabilize single-run initialization variance on compact low-prevalence validation splits, standard Cyber-JEV averages decision margins across five independent random-seed runs (individual seed AUROCs span 0.795–0.820, mean 0.805), alongside reporting the validation-selected single checkpoint (0.820 AUROC).

IV-B Benchmarks, Operating Regimes, and Statistical Protocol

Main Benchmark and Unseen Patch Suites. The primary benchmark contains 7,270 functions across 57 open-source projects from PrimeVul, DiverseVul, and CVEfixes (322 vulnerable functions, 4.43% natural prevalence), reflecting realistic power-law ecosystems spanning foundational infrastructure and 52 medium/long-tail repositories, and embedding 271 vulnerability–patch pairs (T271). To test out-of-distribution generalization on unseen repositories, we evaluate two external patch suites from TitanVul [32]: A72 (72 pairs) and P309 (309 pairs). To quantify surface benchmark cues, we also evaluate a token-length heuristic and a logistic regression fit on validation/calibration data using token length plus benchmark subset-tag indicators (PrimeVul, DiverseVul, or CVEfixes).

Commercial Baseline and Operational Regimes. We query Jev 1.13 [1, 2] via its official API using the identical prompt; its default threshold (p>0.5p>0.5) triggers 4,031 alerts. We evaluate four practical false-positive rate (FPR) and recall regimes: (1) strict low-FPR audit (recall at 1% and 5% FPR, R@1% and R@5%, a ranking measure whose threshold is placed with test labels); and, without using test labels, (2) equal alert budget (matching Jev’s 4,031 alerts); (3) calibration-locked screening (threshold locked on 245 calibration negatives for FPR≤0.50\text{FPR}\leq 0.50); and (4) high-recall noise reduction (threshold aligned to Jev’s recall on validation/calibration positives). Statistical inference uses 2,000-resample 95% project-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) across the 57 projects and exact McNemar tests on patch pairs.

V Comparison with Jev and Error Analysis

V-A Head-to-Head Triage Performance Across Operational Regimes

Table III and Fig. 2 summarize main benchmark performance. Zero-shot Qwen3.5-4B reaches only 0.640 AUROC, confirming that general code pretraining alone is inadequate for vulnerability triage. Cyber-JEV significantly outperforms Jev 1.13 across all four primary ranking metrics (all 95% project-cluster CIs exclude zero): AUROC improves from 0.743 to 0.814, average precision (AP) nearly doubles from 0.101 to 0.197 (+95% relative), and length-stratified AUROC rises from 0.706 to 0.768. Crucially, while biased ablations in the middle block of Table III (such as source logit adjustment at 0.825 AUROC) achieve high macroscopic scores, they collapse on T271 patch pairs (28.4%); Cyber-JEV combines strong global ranking with improved patch sensitivity.

Table IV translates these metrics into exact true positives (TP), missed defects (false negatives, FN), false alarms (false positives, FP), and true negatives (TN) across all 322 vulnerable and 6,948 benign test functions. At a 1% FPR cap, Cyber-JEV catches 33 vulnerabilities versus 7 for Jev (4.6×\times the recall; tied scores leave Jev at 58 of the 69 allowed false alarms); under Jev’s 4,031-alert budget, it cuts missed vulnerabilities from 39 to 16; at its calibration-locked threshold, it finds 18 more defects with 131 fewer false alarms than Jev’s default point (Fig. 2, left); and when aligning recall on validation/calibration positives, it cuts false alarms from 3,748 to 2,466 (34.2%) at 81.7% test recall versus 87.9% for Jev, a recall difference that is not statistically significant, whereas reference-pool-only training achieves no significant FP reduction.

V-B Root-Cause Analysis of False Positives and False Negatives

Analyzing model predictions and representation probes identifies three core mechanisms behind false positives (FP) and two likely sources of false negatives (FN):

1) FP Driver 1: Repository Style and File-Context Spillover. In Fig. 3 (left), naive uncompleted mixing allows a linear probe to decode source identity from last-layer embeddings at 0.869 AUROC, causing the model to falsely flag 94.0% of the 1,924 held-out benign external same-file functions. Pairing patched versions without unchanged same-file functions still leaves this cross-source FPR at 89.9%. Full PMC and HYB cut cross-source FPR to 41.5%, and adding patched and unchanged functions moves the held-out functions toward the benchmark negatives (Fig. 3, right), suppressing false alarms caused by unfamiliar project conventions or co-location in risky files.

2) FP Driver 2: Function Length and Complexity Bias. Table III shows that logistic regression on token length and subset tags reaches 0.734 AUROC overall yet drops to 0.615 within length quintiles. Similarly, Jev 1.13 drops from 0.743 to 0.706 within length strata, consistent with a bias toward long functions. Cyber-JEV sustains 0.768 length-stratified AUROC, curbing complexity-driven false alarms.

3) FP Driver 3: Residual High-Risk Context and Score Ties on Patched Code. Under permissive high-recall binary thresholds (>85%>85\% recall), because security patches alter only a few lines while leaving the surrounding pointer arithmetic and buffer operations unchanged, any coarse binary threshold flags both pre-fix and post-fix versions as belonging to high-risk modules. Crucially, however, Jev 1.13 outputs exact tied probabilities on 18.8% (51/271) of T271 pairs—its apparent 50.7% score includes 9.4 percentage points of half-credit from ties, corresponding to a strict win rate of only 41.3% (112/271). Cyber-JEV produces continuous tie-free margins achieving a 47.6% strict win rate (+6.3 points over Jev), ranking unpatched defects ahead of repaired code in priority queues.

4) FN Drivers and Single-Function Screening Boundaries. The 16 missed defects at equal alert budget (5.0% FN) and marginal FN increases under noise reduction have not been inspected one by one; likely sources are (i) inter-procedural vulnerabilities governed by caller argument validation or cross-function memory lifecycles invisible within a single function body, and (ii) compact logic flaws in short functions lacking canonical memory APIs, which receive conservative scores under mild score–length correlation (Spearman ρ=0.46\rho=0.46).

VI Shortcut Diagnostics and Component Ablations

Table V jointly evaluates cross-source negative separation (AUROC distinguishing held-out external benign functions from benchmark negatives, where 0.500 is ideal; notably, an unlabeled version computed against all pooled benchmark functions matches the labeled metric within 0.015 across all models, offering a zero-label pre-deployment check) and patch-pair ranking accuracy on T271 and unseen TitanVul suites A72 and P309; length-stratified AUROC is reported in Table III.

Overcoming Anti-Patch Bias. Baselines lacking patch contrasts systematically invert minimal fixes: reference-pool fine-tuning and source logit adjustment rank the vulnerable version higher on only 32.8% and 28.4% of T271 pairs, and 33.3% and 23.6% of unseen A72 pairs (persisting even on the 51 pairs where patching does not increase length). Compared with reference-pool training, full Cyber-JEV maintains 0.814 global AUROC and 0.433 source separation while boosting pair accuracy by +14.8, +29.2, and +14.9 percentage points on T271, A72, and P309 (all p<10−3p<10^{-3} via exact McNemar test).

Causal Direction of Contrastive Supervision. The random-label group baseline preserves identical group members and compute as HYB but randomly assigns which member in each group is treated as positive (corrupting 69% of groups). Cyber-JEV beats this baseline on all 5 out of 5 random seeds (+0.055 mean single-seed AUROC gain; 0.814 vs. 0.776 ensemble AUROC, hierarchical 95% CI [+0.019,+0.095][+0.019,+0.095]), while random group labels collapse T271 accuracy to 31.7%.

Role of Matched Negatives and Weight λ\lambda. Removing patched versions (HYB: in-file context only) drops pair accuracy to 34.7%–35.6%, confirming that patched versions drive fine-grained repair sensitivity; two-member {x+,xpatch}\{x^{+},x^{\text{patch}}\} groups focus conditional gradients solely on the patch edit, reaching 55.7%, 80.6%, and 63.1% pair accuracy. Meanwhile, unchanged same-file functions supply benign repository context and stabilize full-data representations (lifting two-epoch full-data ranking AUROC from 0.627 to 0.700). Indiscriminate negative volume, however, dilutes repair supervision: adding all 39,402 same-file functions into cross-entropy lowers T271 accuracy to 37.6%. Varying λ\lambda in (3) traces a smooth frontier: λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 lowers T271 to 35.8%, whereas λ=2.0\lambda=2.0 raises T271 to 52.8% and A72 to 79.2% at a −0.026-0.026 global AUROC trade-off. Default λ=1.0,K=2\lambda=1.0,K=2 balances global screening and local repair sensitivity.

VII Use in Software Review

Workflow for changing code. For a pull request, adjacent versions or a sequence of releases, Cyber-JEV fits a five-step loop. First, extract the functions that changed. Second, score each new version. Third, score its previous version as a reference for the change: a rise suggests the change added risk, but the absolute score of the new version stays in the ranking, so that an already risky function is not dropped because its score barely moved. Fourth, sort by score and cut at the review budget, for example the number of functions a team can inspect per release. Fifth, give the selected functions deeper checks with queries, rules, a reviewer or a review assistant.

Evidence and outlook. The pair sets contain code before and after real historical fixes, so they measure the sensitivity to version changes that the third step relies on. They are not pull requests in progress. We have not deployed the loop in continuous integration, run it across consecutive releases, or used it to find new vulnerabilities; these remain to be shown.

Efficiency. A single model reads a function once and returns its score from one forward pass. It does not generate an explanation token by token or call repository tools. Functions are independent, so they can be scored in batches. When the input, model weights and preprocessing are fixed, the score of an unchanged function can be reused from a cache across versions. The main ensemble costs five forward passes per function; the selected single model costs one and reaches an AUROC of 0.820. We did not measure throughput against other tools.

Relation to existing tools. CodeQL builds a database from the code, runs queries over it and reports code-scanning alerts [33]; its incremental analysis reuses a cached database and can restrict alerts to lines that a pull request adds or modifies [34]. Semgrep runs rule sets and offers diff-aware scans of the files changed in a pull request [35]. Copilot code review gathers repository context, comments on a pull request and suggests fixes, and its documentation advises adding a human review [36]. Incremental scanning is thus not specific to our approach. A learned score adds a different output: one number per function that a program can sort, threshold and cap at a budget, produced by an open-weight model that can run on local hardware, so the code need not leave the organization. Rules and review comments explain a finding, whereas the score only orders work, which fits the role of a first stage in front of these tools. We make no claim about relative speed or accuracy, because we did not compare the tools on the same task in the same environment.

VIII Related Work

Code Vulnerability Detection and Fast Decision Models. Graph neural networks and pretrained code encoders have been widely explored for function- and line-level vulnerability detection [37, 38, 39], while recent studies audit large language models on security reasoning [4, 3]. Empirical analyses highlight that deduplication, realistic low prevalence, and minimal patch pairs expose shortcut reliance [7, 8, 5, 32]. Building on Jev’s single-step probabilistic interface [1, 2], Cyber-JEV resolves the data and optimization challenges of adapting open language models to source-code triage.

Shortcut Mitigation and Contrastive Code Learning. Dataset bias and shortcut learning pervade security machine learning [40, 41, 42]. Distributionally robust optimization [12], invariant risk minimization [13], domain-adversarial networks [43], and CausalVul [44] require both classes per environment, while positive-unlabeled learning [45, 46] and logit adjustment [14] adjust class priors without teaching patch sensitivity. Unlike contrastive code models using generic in-batch negatives [23, 47], Cyber-JEV unites conditional likelihood [15, 18] with commit-matched hard-negative ranking [22, 20] while anchoring global probabilities on a clean reference pool.

IX Conclusion

We introduced Cyber-JEV, a matched contrastive fine-tuning framework that adapts open-weight language models to fast single-pass source-code vulnerability triage. Provenance-Matched Completion turns positive-only vulnerability records into hash-verified groups of vulnerable, patched, and unchanged same-file functions, and the Anchored-Contrastive Hybrid Loss trains these groups through within-group ranking while keeping cross-entropy on a reference pool with natural labels. On a 7,270-function benchmark, the five-model Cyber-JEV ensemble outperforms Jev 1.13 on all four ranking measures, finds 33 instead of 7 vulnerabilities at a 1% false-positive rate, and reduces missed vulnerabilities from 39 to 16 under the same 4,031-alert budget. It also ranks vulnerable code above its patched version 14.8 to 29.2 percentage points more often than reference-pool fine-tuning on three suites of real fixes. Because each score comes from one forward pass over one function, Cyber-JEV can serve as a first-stage filter that orders the changed functions of pull requests and releases before deeper analysis. Future work will evaluate this workflow on live pull requests and consecutive releases.
